title: Najdorf Sicilian: why ...a6, two structures, two plans
outcomes: Says what 5...a6 does (it attacks b5) and finds the flaw in 6.Nb5
Tells the ...e6 and ...e5 structures apart by one pawn and names the d5 outpost in the second
Finds a move that fits the Be3 and f3 set-up and one that fits the Bg5 and f4 set-up, for either colour
Reads opening counts as results of games, with source and sample size, and not as verdicts

steps.text: **The Najdorf Sicilian.** After 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3, Black plays **5...a6**. The opening data we ship names this position *Sicilian Defense: Najdorf Variation* (ECO B90). This lesson covers only what belongs to this opening: why the a-pawn moves, two pawn set-ups, and one plan for each side. Engine numbers are evidence at depth 16, not proof; game counts are results of games, not evaluations.

steps.text: **What strong players chose** (results of games, not evaluations). Our file holds 329,379 games between players both rated 2500 or more (2012 to 2026). After 5...a6 White chose **6.Be3** in 2,669 games (784 White wins, 1,257 draws, 628 Black wins) and **6.Bg5** in 1,589 (575, 564, 450). Next most played: 6.Be2 1,371 and 6.h3 1,286. Counts say what was played and how it scored, not which move is stronger.

steps.prompt: After 6.Be3 Black won 628 of 2,669 master games; after 6.Bg5 Black won 450 of 1,589. Before you decide: do these counts show that one move is stronger?

fields.label: My answer:

no, they only show how those games ended

steps.text: **Online games** (Lichess standard rated, September 2026 sample of 4,752,291 games, first 16 plies). Games reaching 5...a6: 155 in the 1100-1300 band and 4,372 in the 2100+ (online) band. 6.Bg5 followed in 33 and 1,088 of them; 6.Be3 in 21 and 994; in the 1100-1300 band 6.Bd3 followed in 31. These are online counts, not master theory, and the two bands differ in size.

steps.text: **Two set-ups.** After 6.Be3, Black's two most common pawn moves in our master data are ...e5 and ...e6 (see the counts later). With **...e6** no black pawn attacks White's knight on d4 and the pawn on e6 guards d5. With **...e5** the pawn attacks that knight, and d5 becomes a square no black pawn can ever guard, because Black's c-pawn is gone. Study both boards, then tap White's outpost.

claims.statement: The d-file is half-open for White and the c-file half-open for Black.
White has no outpost square here.

steps.text: **White's set-up with 6.Be3.** The opening data names the position after 6.Be3 *Najdorf Variation, English Attack*. In master games Black replied ...e5 1,546 times, ...Ng4 673 and ...e6 370. Ideas that go with ...e6 are f3, Qd2, long castling and a g4 pawn advance. That list is a plan. The engine checks only the first move of the line below and the tasks that follow. Step through one line.

steps.text: **White's set-up with 6.Bg5.** In master games Black replied ...e6 966 times and ...Nbd7 592. After 6...e6 the usual follow-up in this lesson is a pawn move that attacks e5, with the queen coming to d2 or f3 only after that pawn move. The engine checks only that moves score close to its top choice. Find White's move.

steps.text: **A plan belongs to a structure.** A move from one set-up can be a mistake in another. Two questions before you borrow a move: what does Black's last pawn move attack, and does my plan still make sense there? Next, a mistake for each colour. The verdicts are engine evidence at depth 16.

**When this holds.** *Rule of thumb:* the f3, Qd2 and g4 plan goes with ...e6, where no black pawn attacks the knight on d4. After ...e5 the knight must move first and d5 becomes the point of the structure. A plan fails when one feature changes, not when the opening name changes. Here that feature is one black pawn. Predict, then check.
